To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“GTN administration induces an increased accumulation of ADMA in the brain, with a consequent decrease in DDAHA-1 mRNA levels and increased nNOS levels, suggesting a possible role of ADMA in migraine pathogenesis.”
GTN administration induces a significant increase in ADMA levels in brain areas that are activated by GTN, but not in serum.
GTN administration induces changes in the expression of the ADMA-DDAH-1-NOS axis in brain areas known to be involved in migraine pathophysiology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the ADMA-DDHA-NOS axis in the specific areas of the brain following nitroglycerine administration in an animal model.
the study of the ADMA-NO axis in the brain following GTN administration, a well-known animal model of spontaneous-like headache.
the evaluation of the role of asymmetric dimethylarginine, an endogenous inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase, in a model of nitroglycerine-induced migraine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ADMA accumulations in specific brain areas are associated with GTN administration.
the present data provide a new insight in the pathophysiological mechanisms involved in the migraine process, suggesting that ADMA may play a role in the regulation of NO synthesis.

the present findings support the idea that GTN administration in rats is a suitable experimental model of migraine, and suggest that the modulation of the ADMA-DDAH-1 axis may be of interest in the development of new migraine treatments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GTN administration induces a compensatory response in the brain, aimed at limiting the effects of excessive local availability of nitric oxide.
ADMA accumulations are involved in the migraine pathophysiology and that the inhibition of DADH-1 is a compensatory mechanism to reduce the NO synthesis.
ADMA levels and expression of neuronal NOS increased in the hypothalamic area and medulla after nitroglycerine administration, while DDAH- 1 expression decreased in these brain regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GTN administration induces a compensatory response of the ADMA/DDHA-NOS axis in the brain that is specific to brain areas known to be involved in migraine pathophysiology.
ADMA is involved in GTN-induced headache and that it could represent a novel target for migraine prevention.
the modulation of NO synthesis may be more complex than previously thought.
